analysis.one_liner: Replaced private health insurance with a state-run universal health program funded by payroll and income taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill had 9 House sponsors and no hearings or votes; it was referred to four House committees and a subcommittee in 2009 and never advanced during the health care debate that produced the ACA instead.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have replaced Medicare, Medicaid, SCHIP, the federal employee insurance program, and TRICARE coverage for service members' families with a universal state-run health program covering hospital care, doctors, prescription drugs, dental, mental health, and long-term care with no deductibles or copays on most services. It banned duplicate private insurance, moved hospitals to set annual budgets, and paid for it with new employer payroll and income-based taxes into a trust fund. It never received a hearing, markup, or vote in the 111th Congress, which instead enacted the Affordable Care Act.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident who is a citizen, national, or lawful permanent resident would be enrolled automatically in a state health security program [S2][S3]. The benefit package covers hospital, physician, prescription drugs, dental, mental health, hospice, home health, and long-term care [S3]. Most acute and preventive care would carry no deductibles, copays, or coinsurance, with reduced long-term care cost-sharing for low-income enrollees [S3]. Coverage would be portable across states, and no one could be charged more than the program rate (no balance billing) [S3]. The unemployed, self-employed, and people with preexisting conditions would no longer depend on an employer plan or purchase insurance on a market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: All U.S. citizens and lawful residents

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a universal entitlement to health care for every U.S. citizen, national, or lawful resident alien, with automatic enrollment at birth and immigration

Covers hospital care, practitioner services, prescription drugs, dental, mental health and substance abuse treatment, long-term and hospice care, with no deductibles or copays on most acute and preventive benefits
Prohibits balance billing so no provider can charge more than the approved rate, and bars the sale of duplicate private health insurance in each state
Funds the program through a new employer payroll tax and a health care income tax into an American Health Security Trust Fund, replacing employer-based premiums with public financing
Pays hospitals on approved global budgets and pays practitioners on a fee schedule, an approach designed to cap total health spending rather than pay per service
Continues veterans' medical benefits under title 38 and Indian Health Service coverage unchanged

analysis.who_pays: Employers would pay a new payroll tax, and higher-income households would pay a new health care income tax into the American Health Security Trust Fund [S3]. The health insurance industry would lose its role as the payer for most health care: the bill eliminates Medicare, Medicaid, SCHIP, FEHB, and CHAMPUS benefits and prohibits selling duplicate coverage in each state [S2][S3]. Private employers could still add extra benefits on top [S3].

drawbacks.text: Creates a new employer payroll tax and a health care income tax to fund the program, a large new financing burden replacing existing premium payments
Terminates Medicare, Medicaid, SCHIP, federal employee health coverage (FEHB), and CHAMPUS military family coverage as of the end of 2010, a total restructuring of programs covering tens of millions
Ends ERISA continuation coverage (COBRA) and other group plan requirements, eliminating the employer-based insurance framework many workers relied on
States must prohibit the sale of private insurance that duplicates covered benefits, removing choice of private coverage
It competed with the ACA in a single session, and its single-payer design did not attract the 60-vote Senate coalition the ACA did; its own co-sponsor count never exceeded 8

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give every lawful resident comprehensive coverage with essentially no out-of-pocket cost, ending medical debt and coverage loss tied to jobs. The tradeoff is the financing: a new payroll tax on employers and an income-based tax would replace premiums rather than add to them, and the elimination of Medicare, Medicaid, and FEHB would be a wrenching one-year transition. Honest supporters and critics alike agreed this was the largest health-system reorganization ever proposed in Congress; the cost and disruption of that transition was the strongest good-faith objection.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to four House committees on the day it was introduced and to a subcommittee the next day; it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 111th Congress ended [S1][S5].

narrative.text: The American Health Security Act of 2009 was introduced on February 25, 2009 by Rep. Jim McDermott with 8 co-sponsors
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Oversight and Government Reform, and Armed Services committees, and on February 26 to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee
No hearings, markups, votes, or further action are recorded for the bill during the 111th Congress
The Congress instead passed the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act in 2010, which expanded coverage through private insurers and exchanges rather than a single public program

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, employers that sponsor health coverage, and providers who kept the existing payment system were better off because the bill never advanced; the ACA that passed in its place kept private insurers as the channel for coverage expansion.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and incumbent health programs kept their roles

for.what_they_did: Introduced the American Health Security Act of 2009 on February 25, 2009

for.name: 8 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Co-sponsored the bill alongside the sponsor; the bill was introduced by McDermott with seven other House members (Engel, Farr, Hinchey, Kucinich, Dicks, Lee, Olver)

against.name: House Democratic leadership and committee chairs
against.role: Controlled floor and committee calendars (D majority, 253 of 435 seats)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or floor vote on the bill during the 111th Congress; the bill sat in four committees and a subcommittee from February 25, 2009 until the Congress ended

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 26, 2009 and took no recorded action on the bill

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.what_they_did: Would have lost the individual, employer, Medicare Advantage, Medicaid managed care, FEHB, and TRICARE-related markets under a single public program; the bill explicitly prohibited duplicate private coverage

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors were Democrats, and the bill never moved in a Democratic-controlled House; no Republican co-sponsor ever signed on [S4].

industries.note: The bill eliminates Medicare, Medicaid, SCHIP, FEHB, and CHAMPUS and prohibits the sale of duplicate private insurance in each state, removing the industry's role as the payer for most American health care. Insurers would be confined to supplemental benefits outside the public program [S2][S3].

Employers would pay a new payroll tax but shed the cost and administration of employer health plans; large employers with good plans could still add supplemental benefits. The bill repeals ERISA and COBRA requirements that structure employer plans [S3].

Providers would be paid on global budgets and a fee schedule with no balance billing, guaranteeing payment for every lawful resident while capping their revenue; hospitals gain universal coverage but lose the ability to bill above the approved rate.

Prescription drugs would be paid under a state fee schedule set by the program rather than negotiated with private insurers, a structure insurers historically used to leverage lower drug prices; no duplicate private drug coverage would be allowed.
